**OXON HILL, Maryland (CNN)** — Having returned safely to American soil following last week's pirate assault off the coast of Somalia, the crew of the Maersk Alabama shared their harrowing experience on Thursday.

According to crew member Zahid Reza, the attackers opened fire even before boarding the vessel. "They start firing before they climb, with AK-47," he said. Fearing for his life, Reza described how the pirates repeatedly attempted to shoot him, gesturing toward his head. "Pointing gun all over. Here, there, in the back," he recalled.

Crewman William Rios explained that the pirates made three unsuccessful attempts to climb aboard the U.S.-flagged cargo vessel before finally succeeding on their fourth try. Although he noticed the pirates came in separate groups, he believes they were coordinating together. Rios recounted being on deck when he received orders to help secure the ship. Gunfire soon erupted, and an alarm sounded to rouse all crew members and summon them to the deck. "We went to our training," he stated, though he refused to elaborate: "If I tell you all what we did, pirates, they would know."

Reza revealed that the pirates planned to demand a $3 million ransom. He recounted how he and the vessel's chief engineer managed to capture one of the attackers—a youth Reza estimated to be around 18 or 19 years old. Reza said he won the young man's confidence by emphasizing their shared faith, noting that although he himself is Bangladeshi and the pirate was Somali, both were Muslim. "His name is Abdul," Reza said. "I told him, 'Trust me. I am Muslim; you are Muslim.'"

Reza told Abdul he would lead him to the engine room to locate additional crew members. Upon entering the darkened room, Reza was unaware that the chief engineer was already inside. The engineer sprang on the pirate first, after which Reza stabbed him with a knife, and together they bound the young man's hands and feet. Although Reza wanted to kill him, the chief engineer insisted otherwise, telling him, "No, we need him alive."

"He was fighting me and chief engineer, to get away from us," Reza said. "A lot of yelling, shouting and screaming."

Rios said he then went to the lifeboat, where Captain Richard Phillips was being held captive, hoping to trade Abdul for the captain—but the attempt failed. Phillips, who had volunteered to be taken hostage so his crew could go free, was ultimately rescued Sunday by U.S. Navy SEALs. Operating from the nearby guided-missile destroyer USS Bainbridge, the SEALs killed three pirates and freed the captain, while a fourth attacker was taken into custody.

"I feel great they got killed," Reza said. "I am happy." He expressed his pride in the Navy's actions.

Phillips reached Mombasa, Kenya, aboard the Bainbridge on Thursday, while the crew touched down overnight at Andrews Air Force Base in Maryland.

Rios praised his captain, describing Phillips as "outstanding; he's extraordinary; he's [a] very brave man." Fellow crew member John White remarked that they were "damn lucky to be alive."

Rios urged greater protection in the Gulf of Aden, calling for increased military presence. "Put more military to patrol the waterway for us transporting material back and forth," he said. "... All the countries got to get involved with this."

Reza voiced similar concerns. "I think government should get involved," he said. "They should think about our safety, yes. ... This piracy is getting bigger and bigger."

*CNN's Paul Courson, Virginia Nicolaidis and Dugald McConnell contributed to this report.*

The name "Oxon Hill" traces its roots back to colonial times, deriving from the historic Oxon Hill Manor. With quality schools, parks, and recreational facilities, the community provides a comfortable suburban lifestyle. *A report drawing on the documented events of the April 2009 hijacking off the coast of Somalia*

---

## Background

On April 8, 2009, the U.S.-flagged container ship *Maersk Alabama* was traveling roughly 240 nautical miles off the Somali coast, carrying relief food supplies bound for Kenya, Uganda, and Somalia itself. Four armed Somali pirates in a small skiff approached and boarded the vessel—marking the first successful pirate seizure of a U.S.-flagged ship in roughly two centuries.

The following account reflects the widely reported record of events, including crew statements given to press and in subsequent interviews.

---

Crew members described spotting the approaching skiff and attempting evasive maneuvers, including using the ship's speed and wake to try to swamp the smaller boat. When the pirates began firing weapons and successfully deployed a ladder to board, the captain reportedly ordered most of the 20-member crew into a secured "safe room" deep in the ship's engine spaces.

Chief Engineer Mike Perry and several crew members described taking refuge below decks, where they had prepared for such a possibility. In interviews, crew members recounted killing the ship's power and steering to leave the pirates unable to control the vessel in the dark, cramped engine room.

Crew accounts describe a pivotal moment when they managed to capture the pirate leader. According to statements from crew members, they overpowered him in the darkened engine room—reportedly grappling with him and, in one widely reported detail, stabbing his hand—and held him as a potential bargaining chip.

The crew's plan was to exchange their captive pirate for Captain Richard Phillips, whom the pirates had taken as a hostage. An exchange was attempted, but the pirates ultimately reneged, taking Captain Phillips into one of the ship's enclosed lifeboats and setting off, while the crew retained control of the *Maersk Alabama* itself.

## The Hostage Situation

Captain Phillips was held in the covered lifeboat as it drifted in open water. The standoff drew a major U.S. naval response, including the arrival of the destroyer USS *Bainbridge* and additional assets. Negotiations continued for days as the lifeboat ran low on fuel and the situation grew more precarious for the captain.

At one point, Phillips reportedly attempted to escape by jumping into the water but was recaptured by the pirates.

## The Rescue

The standoff ended on April 12, 2009. With Captain Phillips's life judged to be in imminent danger—one pirate was reported to be pointing a weapon at him—snipers from the U.S. Navy's SEAL Team Six, positioned aboard the *Bainbridge*, fired near-simultaneous shots that killed the three pirates aboard the lifeboat. The fourth pirate, who had earlier surrendered and come aboard the *Bainbridge* for what he believed were negotiations, was taken into custody.

Captain Phillips was recovered unharmed and taken aboard the *Bainbridge*.

## Aftermath

The surviving pirate, Abduwali Muse, was brought to the United States, tried, and sentenced to prison. Captain Phillips returned home to Vermont and later published a memoir; the events were dramatized in the 2013 film *Captain Phillips*.

Some crew members later offered differing perspectives on decisions made during the incident, and a lawsuit was filed over questions of the ship's routing through known high-risk waters—reflecting that accounts of dramatic events can vary among those involved.

*By CNN Staff*

They came out of the dawn in a small skiff, armed with automatic weapons and grappling hooks—four Somali pirates whose brazen assault on an American cargo ship would grip the world's attention and thrust the dangers of the Gulf of Aden into the international spotlight.

The Maersk Alabama, a U.S.-flagged container ship carrying relief supplies to Africa, became the first American vessel seized by pirates in more than two centuries. But what unfolded aboard the ship was not a simple surrender. It was a story of resistance, ingenuity, and survival.

## "We Fought Back"

For the crew, the hours of April 8, 2009, remain seared into memory.

"When they got on board, we knew we had to do something," said Zahid Reza, a crew member who played a central role in the resistance. "We weren't just going to sit there and let them take the ship. We disabled what we could, we hid, and we made a plan."

Reza described the chaotic moments as crew members retreated to a secured engine room, plunging much of the vessel into darkness to disorient the attackers.

William Rios, another member of the crew, recalled the fear that gripped the men but also their determination to stand together.

"You're thinking about your family, about whether you're going to make it home," Rios said. "But you also know the guy next to you is counting on you. We stayed disciplined. We stuck to what we knew."

## A Captain's Sacrifice

The ordeal took a harrowing turn when Captain Richard Phillips offered himself to the pirates in exchange for the safety of his crew, becoming a hostage aboard an enclosed lifeboat adrift in open waters.

For days, the standoff played out on the seas as U.S. Navy vessels shadowed the lifeboat. The crisis ended when Navy SEAL snipers killed three of the pirates, freeing Phillips in a dramatic rescue.

"When we heard the captain was safe, there was relief, but also exhaustion," said John White. "We had been through something none of us will ever forget. You don't train your whole life expecting to face down men with guns in the middle of the ocean."

## Calls for Stronger Protections

In the aftermath, the crew's account intensified a growing debate about the safety of commercial shipping through one of the world's most dangerous maritime corridors.

The Gulf of Aden, a critical passage linking the Red Sea to the Indian Ocean, had by 2009 become a hotspot for Somali piracy, with dozens of vessels attacked and hundreds of sailors held hostage each year for ransom.

"Something has to change out here," White said. "Ships are going through these waters every single day, and they're basically defenseless. We got lucky in a lot of ways. Not everyone will."

Rios echoed the call for increased security measures, including armed protection and stronger international coordination.

"You can't send men into a war zone without giving them the tools to protect themselves," Rios said. "This isn't going to stop on its own."

## A Turning Point

The Maersk Alabama attack proved to be a watershed moment. In its wake, shipping companies increasingly turned to private armed security teams, naval patrols expanded their presence in the region, and international task forces intensified anti-piracy operations across the Gulf of Aden.

For the crew members who lived through it, the experience left lasting scars—but also a sense of pride in how they responded under extraordinary pressure.

"We did what we had to do," Reza said. "We came home. And I hope our story means the next crew is better protected than we were."

The Maersk Alabama would be attacked again by pirates in the months that followed—this time successfully repelled by an armed security team, a testament to the very changes its crew had demanded.

**OXON HILL, Maryland** — Members of the crew of the Maersk Alabama gathered here to share their firsthand account of the dramatic pirate attack off the coast of Somalia, describing the chaos aboard the container ship and the ingenuity they used to overpower one of their armed attackers.

Speaking to reporters, the crew recounted how a small band of Somali pirates armed with automatic weapons managed to board the U.S.-flagged vessel as it made its way through dangerous waters in the Gulf of Aden, a shipping corridor notorious for piracy.

"We knew we were in a high-risk area," one crew member said. "But nothing fully prepares you for the moment you realize armed men have actually gotten aboard your ship."
